items.title: Focus Question: A manufacturer wants to build one diode and one npn transistor on a silicon chip. How are the semiconductor regions prepared to make these components?

body.html: Pure silicon is doped with donor atoms (such as phosphorus) to make n-type regions and with acceptor atoms (such as boron) to make p-type regions. A single p-n junction forms a diode; an n-p-n sandwich (with a very thin middle layer) forms an npn transistor. Doping through patterned masks puts the regions only where they are wanted, and a metal such as aluminum deposited on the surface makes the conducting pathways.

answer.html: Doping selected regions of silicon with donor or acceptor atoms makes n-type and p-type layers; one p-n junction is a diode, and an n-p-n sandwich with a thin base is a transistor.

check.html: This matches the lesson summary: junctions make diodes, three-layer sandwiches make transistors.

items.title: Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question (Lesson 2)

question.html: Work (model response): Evidence from this lesson for how hearing aids shrank: transistors replaced bulky, hot, short-lived vacuum tubes; they use little power, so a tiny battery is enough; diodes, transistors, and resistors can all be made by doping the same silicon crystal, so an entire amplifier fits on one chip, with components less than a micrometer across.

answer.html: Solid-state transistors and integrated circuits are the lesson's evidence for how hearing aids (and computers) became small.

Problem 1 (Lesson 2, Example 4 Practice 1): A silicon diode (𝛥𝑉𝑑= 0.70 V) is in series with a 220 Ω resistor. What battery potential difference gives a current of 6.5 mA?

body.html: 𝐼= 6.5 mA = 0.0065 A, 𝑅= 220 𝛺, 𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑑</sub>= 0.70 V. Find 𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑏</sub>.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑏</sub>≈2.1 V

check.html: The battery must supply the resistor's drop plus the diode's 0.70 V, so it exceeds 0.70 V.

items.title: 2 (Example 4 Practice 2): A germanium diode with a 0.30 V drop is in series with a 680 Ω resistor. What battery potential difference gives a current of 9.0 mA?

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑏</sub>≈6.4 V

check.html: The resistor takes almost all of the battery voltage because the germanium drop is small.

items.title: 3 (Example 4 Practice 3): Three identical silicon diodes (0.70 V each) are connected in series with a 150 Ω resistor. What battery potential difference gives a current of 8.0 mA?

body.html: Each diode drops 0.70 V; 𝐼= 0.0080 A; 𝑅= 150 𝛺.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑏</sub>≈3.3 V

check.html: The three diodes together take more of the voltage than the resistor does.

items.title: 4 (Example 4 Practice 4): How should the three diodes in problem 3 be connected to the battery?

body.html: All three must be forward-biased, so they point the same way along the current path: the n- side (bar) of one diode connects to the p-side of the next, and the p-side of the first diode faces the positive battery terminal.

answer.html: In series, all facing the same direction, with the p-end of the first diode toward the battery's positive terminal and the n-end of the last toward the negative terminal (through the resistor).

check.html: Conventional current then flows with the arrow of each diode symbol.

items.title: 5 (Example 4 Practice 5, Challenge): In the circuit of problem 3, the middle diode is accidentally installed backward. What happens to the current and to the voltages?

body.html: A reverse-biased diode acts as a very high resistance; only about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>11</sup> A flows.

The backward diode blocks the circuit, so the current stays near 10<sup>−</sup><sup>11</sup> A instead of 8.0 mA. Almost the whole battery voltage appears across the reversed diode, and almost none across the resistor or the other two diodes. The required 8.0 mA would not flow.

answer.html: Essentially no current flows (about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>11</sup> A), and nearly all of the battery voltage drops across the reversed diode.

check.html: This matches the reverse-bias behavior described in the lesson.

items.title: Figure 13 prompt: In a circuit diagram, the arrow on the emitter of a transistor points toward the base. What does the arrow mean, and is the transistor npn or pnp?

body.html: The arrow on the emitter marks the direction of conventional (positive) current through the emitter. An arrow pointing toward the base means conventional current flows into the transistor through the emitter. That is the symbol for a pnp transistor.

answer.html: The arrow shows the direction of conventional current in the emitter. Pointing toward the base means current enters at the emitter, so the transistor is pnp. (In an npn transistor the arrow points away from the base.)

check.html: Consistent with the rule that the emitter arrow points in the direction of conventional current.

items.title: Figure 14 prompt: Draw a circuit using a pnp transistor, with a 4.5 V battery and an 82 kΩ resistor in the base circuit and a 9.0 V battery and a 1.2 kΩ resistor in the collector circuit. Show which way conventional current flows

body.html: A pnp transistor works like the npn circuit with both battery polarities reversed. The positive terminal of each battery connects toward the emitter, so the base and collector are more negative than the emitter.

Connect the emitter to the common line joined to both positive terminals. The base battery drives a small current 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub> through the 82 kΩ resistor, and the collector battery drives a larger current 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub> through the 1.2 kΩ resistor. The emitter arrow points toward the base. Conventional current flows from the positive terminals into the emitter (𝐼<sub>𝐸</sub>), and out of the transistor through the base ( 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>) and the collector (𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>), with 𝐼<sub>𝐸</sub>= 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>+ 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>.

answer.html: See the diagram: both batteries have their positive terminals toward the emitter, current enters through the emitter and leaves through the base and the collector.

check.html: Reversing both batteries of the npn circuit gives this pnp circuit.

items.title: Get It? (p. 665): Why is aluminum, instead of phosphorus or boron, used to make the conducting pathways on a chip?

body.html: Phosphorus and boron are dopants; they would make n-type and p-type semiconductor regions, which are not good metallic conductors. Aluminum is a good metallic conductor that can be evaporated in a thin layer to make wire-like paths.

answer.html: Aluminum is a good conductor and works as a wire; phosphorus and boron are dopants that make n-type and p-type semiconductor rather than metallic connections.

check.html: Consistent with the difference between doped regions and conducting pathways in the lesson.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts (Structure and Function): LED circuit and polarity

question.html: A student connects a 5.0 V supply, a 330 Ω resistor, and a green LED (potential difference about 2.1 V when lit) in series, then reverses the LED. Work (expected result, representative; not measured here): With the p-end of the LED toward the positive terminal (through the resistor), the LED lights. The loop rule gives the current:

With the LED reversed, it does not light. In forward bias, electrons from the n-side and holes from the p- side move toward the junction, recombine, and release light. In reverse bias, the carriers move away from the junction, the depletion layer widens, and almost no current flows.

answer.html: Expected result: the forward-biased LED lights with a current of about 8.8 mA; the reversed LED stays dark. The junction's structure lets current pass in only one direction.

check.html: The 8.8 mA is typical for an LED and well below the damaging range, and no light in reverse bias is as expected.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) Problem 1: A sensor produces a weak alternating current. A meter needs a larger one-direction (DC) signal. Which two components can be used, and in what order?

body.html: Pass the AC signal through a diode (a rectifier), which allows current in only one direction, giving a one-directional signal. Then use that signal as the base current of a transistor, which amplifies it into a much larger collector current.

answer.html: First a diode to rectify the AC into DC, then a transistor to amplify the signal.

check.html: Uses the two functions the lesson gives for diodes and transistors.

items.title: 2: A technician measures a diode with an ohmmeter and reads 85 Ω with the leads one way and 4.0 × 107 𝛺 with the leads reversed. Which reading was taken in forward bias, and why?

body.html: Forward bias eliminates the depletion layer, so the diode acts as a low-value resistor. Reverse bias widens the depletion layer, so the diode acts as a very high-value resistor.

answer.html: The 85 Ω reading is forward bias; the 4.0 × 10<sup>7</sup> 𝛺 reading is reverse bias.

check.html: Low resistance means current passes easily, which is forward bias.

items.title: 3: An LED is connected with its n-end toward the positive battery terminal. Will it light? How should it be connected?

body.html: With the n-end toward the positive terminal, the LED is reverse-biased, so almost no current flows and it stays dark. To forward-bias it, the p-end must connect to the positive terminal.

answer.html: It will not light. Reverse the LED so its p-end connects to the positive terminal.

check.html: Matches the forward-bias rule from the lesson.

items.title: 4: In a transistor, the base current is 38 µA and the collector current is 7.1 mA. What is the current gain?

body.html: 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>= 38 𝜇A = 3.8 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> A, 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>= 7.1 mA = 7.1 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> A.

answer.html: current gain = 1.9 × 10<sup>2</sup>

check.html: Within the 50 to 300 range for general-purpose transistors.

items.title: 5: A transistor has a current gain of 140. What is the ratio of emitter current to base current?

body.html: 𝐼<sub>𝐸</sub>= 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>+ 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>, 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>/ 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>= 140.

answer.html: 𝐼<sub>𝐸</sub>/ 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>= 141

check.html: Slightly larger than the gain, since the emitter carries the base current as well.

items.title: 6: A silicon diode (𝛥𝑉𝑑= 0.70 V) is in series with a 68 Ω resistor. What battery potential difference is needed for a current of 25 mA?

body.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑑</sub>= 0.70 V, 𝑅= 68 𝛺, 𝐼= 25 mA.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑏</sub>≈2.4 V

items.title: 7: A silicon diode carrying more than 10 mA is in series with a 240 Ω resistor. The battery potential difference is increased by 2.5 V. (a) By how much do the diode and resistor potential differences change? (b) By how much does the current change?

body.html: Above about 10 mA, the diode voltage stays essentially at 0.70 V, so any change in the battery voltage must appear across the series resistor (loop rule). Work (a): 𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑑</sub> stays about 0.70 V, so it changes by about 0 V. Then 𝛥(𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑏</sub>) = 𝛥(𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑅</sub>) + 𝛥(𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑑</sub>), so 𝛥(𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑅</sub>) = 2.5 V −0 = 2.5 V. Work (b):

answer.html: The diode voltage changes by about 0 V (stays about 0.70 V); the resistor voltage increases by 2.5 V.
The current increases by about 10 mA.

check.html: The 2.5 V increase is all across the resistor; 10 mA × 240 𝛺= 2.5 V.

items.title: 8 (Critical Thinking): Can a pnp transistor be replaced by two separate diodes connected by their n-terminals?

body.html: Two separate diodes joined at their n-ends would form the same p-n-n-p sequence of junctions, and each diode alone conducts in one direction. But the transistor works because the base is very thin and shared by both junctions: carriers injected from the emitter cross the thin base into the collector, and the base current controls the collector current. Two separate diodes have a thick connecting region where electrons and holes recombine, and the two junctions do not interact, so there is no current amplification.

answer.html: No. Two diodes joined at their n-terminals have the same polarity arrangement but lack the single thin base shared by two junctions, so they cannot amplify current.

check.html: The two-diode picture is only a rough model; the very thin base is part of both junctions.

items.title: 1: How would each quantity change when the switch is closed? (a) the base current (b) the collector current (c) the voltmeter reading

body.html: With the switch open, there is no base current, so the transistor is off. Closing the switch forward-biases the base-emitter junction; a base current flows, and the collector current is 180 times larger.
Switch open: 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>= 0, so 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>= 0, there is no drop across the 1200 𝛺 resistor, and the voltmeter reads the full 12 V. Switch closed:

answer.html: The base current increases from 0 to about 2.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> A (25 µA).
The collector current increases from 0 to about 4.6 mA.
The voltmeter reading decreases from 12 V to about 6.5 V.

check.html: The collector-emitter voltage is positive, so the transistor is still amplifying (not saturated); 5.5 + 6.5 = 12 V.

items.title: 2: Evidence and reasoning: justify your answers with calculations

body.html: The calculations above are the justification. The reasoning in words: a small base current (about 25 µA) controls a collector current 180 times larger (about 4.6 mA). That collector current produces a large voltage drop across 𝑅<sub>𝐶</sub> (loop rule), which leaves less of the 12 V battery across the transistor, so the voltmeter reading falls.

answer.html: The base current rises to about 25 µA, the collector current to about 4.6 mA, and the voltmeter reading falls from 12 V to about 6.5 V, justified by 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>= (4.5 −0.70) / 𝑅<sub>𝐵</sub>, 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>= 180 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>, and the loop rule.

check.html: Units: V/Ω = A, and A × Ω = V.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts (Structure and Function): LED circuit and polarity

question.html: Work (expected result, representative; not measured here): With the battery connected one way, the LED lights; reversed, it does not. The light shows that charges are moving only when the LED is forward-biased: the positive terminal is connected (through the resistor) to the p-end. Then electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side move toward the junction, recombine, and release energy as light. In reverse bias, the carriers move away from the junction, the depletion layer widens, and almost no current flows.

answer.html: The lit LED is forward-biased (positive terminal to the p-end); the unlit one is reverse- biased. The junction's structure lets current pass in only one direction.

check.html: An LED lights only when the current is large enough, so no light in reverse bias is as expected.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) Problem 1: Make a larger DC signal from a low-current AC signal

body.html: Pass the AC signal through a diode (a rectifier), which allows current in only one direction and so gives a one-directional (DC) signal. Then use the rectified signal as the base current of a transistor; the transistor amplifies it into a much larger collector current.

answer.html: Rectify with a diode to convert AC to DC, then feed the signal to the base of a transistor to amplify it.

check.html: Uses the two functions the lesson gives for diodes and transistors.

items.title: 2: Forward-biased versus reverse-biased resistance

body.html: Forward bias eliminates the depletion layer and the diode behaves like a low-value resistor. Reverse bias widens the depletion layer and the diode acts as a very high-value resistor (current about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>11</sup> A).

answer.html: Forward-biased: low resistance; reverse-biased: very high resistance.

check.html: Matches Figure 10's caption.

items.title: 3: LED polarity

body.html: The diode must be forward-biased, so the p-end connects to the positive battery terminal.

items.title: 7: Battery voltage raised by 1 V

body.html: Above about 10 mA, the diode voltage stays essentially at 0.70 V, so any change in the battery voltage must appear across the series resistor (loop rule). Work (a): 𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑑</sub> stays about 0.70 V, so it increases by about 0 V. Then 𝛥(𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑏</sub>) = 𝛥(𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑅</sub>) + 𝛥(𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑑</sub>), so 𝛥(𝛥𝑉<sub>𝑅</sub>) = 1 V −0 = 1 V. Work (b): The resistor's value is not given in the problem text, so the answer is stated in terms of 𝑅 :
For example, 𝑅= 100 𝛺 would give 10 mA.

answer.html: The diode voltage increases by about 0 V (stays about 0.70 V); the resistor voltage increases by about 1 V.
The current increases by 𝛥𝐼= (1 V) / 𝑅 (resistor's value not given).

check.html: The 1 V increase is all across the resistor; a small 𝑅 gives a large current change.

items.title: 8 (Critical Thinking): Replace an npn transistor with two diodes connected by their p- terminals?

body.html: Two separate diodes joined at their p-ends would form the same n-p-p-n sequence of junctions, and each diode alone does conduct in one direction. But the transistor works because the base is very thin and shared by both junctions: carriers injected from the emitter cross the thin base into the collector, and the base current controls the collector current. Two separate diodes have a thick connecting region where electrons and holes recombine, and the two junctions do not interact, so there is no current amplification.

answer.html: No. Two diodes joined at their p-terminals have the same polarity arrangement, but they lack the single thin base shared by two junctions, so they cannot amplify current.

check.html: The text says to think of the junctions as two back-to-back diodes but also stresses that the very thin base is part of both.

items.title: 1: How would each quantity change when the switch is closed?

body.html: With the switch open, there is no base current, so the transistor is off. Closing the switch forward-biases the base-emitter junction; a base current flows, and the collector current is 220 times larger.
Switch open: 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>= 0, so 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>= 0, there is no drop across the 1500 𝛺 resistor, and the voltmeter reads the full 15 V. Switch closed:

answer.html: The base current increases from 0 to about 2.3 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> A (23 µA).
The collector current increases from 0 to about 5.1 mA.
The voltmeter reading decreases from 15 V to about 7.3 V.

check.html: The collector-emitter voltage is positive, so the transistor is still amplifying (not saturated); 7.7 + 7.3 = 15 V.

items.title: 2: Reasoning and calculations

body.html: The calculations above are the justification. The reasoning in words: a small base current (about 23 µA) controls a collector current 220 times larger (about 5.1 mA). That collector current produces a large voltage drop across 𝑅<sub>𝐶</sub> (loop rule), which leaves less of the 15 V battery across the transistor, so the voltmeter reading falls.

answer.html: The base current rises to about 23 µA, the collector current to about 5.1 mA, and the voltmeter reading falls from 15 V to about 7.3 V, justified by 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>= (3.5 −0.70) / 𝑅<sub>𝐵</sub>, 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>= 220 𝐼<sub>𝐵</sub>, and the loop rule.

check.html: Units: V/Ω = A, and A × Ω = V.
